added_claim_errors: Opens by saying the Part B penalty applies to people who go without "creditable coverage". Creditable coverage is the Part D term, so this is imprecise for Part B.

Tells the asker to apply for Part B at retirement with CMS-40B plus CMS-L564 without checking Part A status. CMS-40B is wrong if Part A was also deferred, and the asker may have deferred it under item 3.
Says CMS-L564 is "completed by your employer". The asker completes Section A and the employer completes Section B, so this is incomplete.
Says to sign up for Part D "within 63 days" of losing creditable drug coverage. The Part D SEP is 2 full months. 63 days is the penalty-free gap, so this is a conservative approximation.
Three Medicare.gov URLs are given as citations. None can be checked from the packet, so they are unverifiable. I found no specific error in them.

Says to enroll in "Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan within 63 days if your drug coverage isn't creditable". This is muddled. If the employer drug coverage is not creditable, delaying Part D builds a penalty, so the asker should not wait until leaving the job.
Says that without 40 quarters Part A has "its own late penalty". A Part A premium late penalty exists, but a valid SEP avoids it, so this overstates the risk.

Cites a KFF FAQ about a 65-year-old covered under a working spouse's plan, and an "ARPI" codex page on IRMAA. Neither can be checked from the packet, and the KFF page is a different scenario from the asker's.
Cites a Federal Register URL (FR-2025-11-19, 2025-20251) for the 2026 premium. The $202.90 figure matches the key, but the document number is unverifiable.
Says Part B would cover "little your plan doesn't already cover". This is a broad generalization about an unknown plan.

reasons: Both answers catch the baited premise at the start. Each says that, with about 400 employees and active-employee coverage, the employer plan pays first and Part B can wait without a penalty. Each also gives the 8-month SEP, and each misses the exception for a job or coverage that ends during the IEP. B is stronger on the key's specifics. It states the 2026 premium of $202.90 and about $2,435 a year, which is correct (202.90 x 12 = 2,434.80). It also covers the 6-month Medigap open enrollment, the Part A backdating of up to 6 months for HSA holders, and the point that taking Part B now is allowed in some cases. A has no premium figure, no Medigap point, and gives the HSA warning without the 6-month backdating. A does name CMS-L564 for the retirement step, but it sends the asker to CMS-40B without conditioning on having Part A, which is a trap error. B names no retirement forms. B is longer, with a repeated bottom line and disclaimer, so it loses on concision. B's Part D wording for the retirement step is also muddled. B still comes out ahead on correctness and usefulness.
